paragraphs: ALE-Bench evaluates whether AI systems can keep improving algorithms for difficult optimization problems. Its tasks come from AtCoder Heuristic Contests, where solutions receive scores rather than simply passing or failing. The problems are computationally hard and have no known exact solution, making the quality of an approximate solution central to evaluation.

The benchmark emphasizes sustained engineering: developing a solution, testing it, interpreting feedback, and refining it over a long period. Its software supports interactive agents that can use test results and visualizations during this process. This setup makes improvement over repeated attempts part of the task, reflecting work involved in applications such as routing, scheduling, production planning, and power-grid balancing.

The reported evaluation finds that frontier language models can perform strongly on particular problems, but remain less consistent than humans across problems and weaker at sustained problem solving. ALE-Bench therefore provides a way to assess both solution quality and the ability to make productive use of a longer engineering process.
neurips-2025-ale-bench-a-benchmark-for-l.tldr: ALE-Bench tests how well AI systems iteratively improve algorithms for difficult optimization problems over long time horizons.

paragraphs: Relative similarity testing asks which of two distributions is closer to a reference distribution. Kernel-based methods make this comparison through a chosen mathematical representation. The paper identifies a problem with first declaring which distribution should be closer and then selecting a kernel: kernel selection can produce a rejection of that preselected hypothesis, making the procedure ill-defined.

The proposed anchor-based maximum discrepancy, or AMD, learns the comparison hypothesis together with the kernel. It searches a space of deep kernels for the largest discrepancy between the two distances to the reference. This makes the choice of representation and the direction of the comparison parts of the same learning problem.

Testing then proceeds in two phases. The first estimates AMD and identifies a candidate hypothesis; the second evaluates its statistical significance. A unified framework supplies thresholds for the different hypotheses the first phase might produce. The authors provide theoretical validation and benchmark experiments supporting effectiveness, addressing how to make adaptive similarity comparisons statistically meaningful.
neurips-2025-anchor-based-maximum-discre.tldr: AMD jointly learns a similarity hypothesis and a deep kernel, then tests the hypothesis’s statistical significance.

paragraphs: Cycle-Sync estimates camera orientations and locations in a single global framework. Its central idea is to emphasize measurements that remain consistent around cycles of camera relationships. Such agreement helps the solver distinguish mutually compatible information from measurements that could distort the overall pose estimate.

The main contribution adapts message-passing least squares, originally developed for group synchronization, to camera localization. The method updates its cycle-consistency calculations using distances estimated in earlier iterations and incorporates a Welsch-type robust loss. It also adds a modular outlier-rejection component inspired by robust subspace recovery and integrates cycle consistency into the rotation-estimation procedure.

The authors establish what they describe as the strongest known deterministic exact-recovery guarantee for camera locations, with the lowest sample complexity to date enabled by cycle consistency alone. This is a recovery guarantee rather than a claim that every input is recoverable. Synthetic and real-data experiments report consistent improvements over leading pose estimators, including full structure-from-motion pipelines, while Cycle-Sync itself avoids bundle adjustment.
neurips-2025-cycle-sync-robust-global-ca.tldr: Cycle-Sync uses cycle-consistent measurements and robust estimation to recover camera poses globally without bundle adjustment.

paragraphs: Graph message-passing networks face two related difficulties: repeated updates can make node representations too similar, while communication bottlenecks can compress information excessively. These problems are known as oversmoothing and oversquashing. The paper argues that globally modifying message passing can help some parts of a graph while harming others, limiting the network’s expressive power.

The authors first analyze oversquashing through the spectral gap, a global graph measure. Their theoretical analysis shows that increasing this gap leads to vanishing gradients with respect to input features, weakening effective message passing. Motivated by this result, they connect local Riemannian geometry to message passing and introduce a nonhomogeneous boundary condition.

Their GBN network builds on the Robin boundary condition to adjust bottlenecks according to local structure, with accompanying theoretical guarantees. Experiments cover graphs where connected nodes tend to be similar and graphs where they tend to differ. The reported results show strong expressiveness and no performance degradation even beyond 256 layers in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-deeper-with-riemannian-geom.tldr: GBN uses local geometric adjustments to address graph message-passing bottlenecks and representation collapse, supporting very deep networks in experiments.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can memorize training examples when data are scarce or insufficiently varied. This paper proposes generating additional graph variations with a diffusion model, without requiring class labels or tying augmentation to one prediction task. The aim is to supply useful diversity while retaining consistency with the underlying graph data.

A graph variational autoencoder first learns a compact representation. Diffusion operates within that representation, which the authors use to improve training stability and reduce computation. When only a fixed amount of augmentation is available, the method selects samples expected to benefit most. Its label-free design also permits augmentation during testing.

The evaluation compares the framework with 30 methods across 12 datasets, covering node classification, link prediction, and graph classification under several learning settings. The authors report better generalization, calibration, resistance to corrupted inputs, and prediction consistency, together with improved robustness against four adversarial attack types. These findings support the value of both generating augmentations efficiently and directing them toward samples where they are most useful.
neurips-2025-diffusion-guided-graph-data.tldr: A label-free latent diffusion framework generates and selectively applies graph augmentations to improve generalization and robustness.

paragraphs: Personalizing a conversation is difficult when an agent has little history about its user. Standard reinforcement learning from human feedback emphasizes qualities such as helpfulness and safety, but those objectives do not directly encourage learning about individual preferences. This paper makes that learning process an explicit part of conversational training.

The method introduces a user model and a curiosity-based intrinsic reward into multi-turn reinforcement learning. The agent receives an incentive to conduct conversations that improve the accuracy of its user model. As it infers more about a person’s traits, it can use that understanding to adapt later interactions, connecting information gathering with personalization across turns.

The authors demonstrate the approach in conversational recommendation and education. They report significantly better personalization in recommendation and conversations adapted to different learning styles, with improved generalization relative to traditional multi-turn reinforcement learning from human feedback. Conversation quality is maintained in the reported evaluations. The findings support rewarding progress in understanding the user as a useful training objective alongside producing good responses.
neurips-2025-enhancing-personalized-mult.tldr: A curiosity reward encourages conversational agents to learn user traits during dialogue and use that knowledge for better personalization.

paragraphs: In federated multi-armed bandits, distributed agents repeatedly choose among shared options and learn which yield better rewards. Their objective is to limit cumulative regret, the reward lost through less effective choices. Because agents communicate through a graph and face bandwidth or privacy constraints, exchanging all observations freely is not available.

The proposed algorithm separates communication into two phases with different purposes. Early, frequent exchanges communicate key decisions for removing inferior options. A second phase refines shared estimates using statistics that are buffered, quantized, and transmitted differentially. This design balances how often agents communicate against how precisely they represent the information they send.

The authors derive tight bounds for both individual and group regret. They report an optimal individual regret bound of O(N⁻¹ log T) and asymptotic agreement with the federated regret lower bound, while reducing communication rounds and transmitted bits. Synthetic experiments across different graph structures and heterogeneous feedback support the approach. The contribution connects learning quality with the actual bit-level cost of collaboration.
neurips-2025-federated-multi-armed-bandi.tldr: A two-phase federated bandit algorithm achieves optimal regret guarantees while reducing communication rounds and transmitted bits.

paragraphs: FEEL benchmarks emotion recognition from electrodermal activity and photoplethysmography signals across 19 public datasets. It evaluates 16 architectures spanning traditional machine learning, deep learning, and self-supervised pretraining. The central question is how reliably methods work when experimental conditions, recording devices, and emotion-labeling practices differ.

The study includes evaluation within individual datasets and transfer between datasets. Fine-tuned contrastive signal-language pretraining models achieve the highest F1 in 71 of 114 arousal and valence classification comparisons, while simpler models remain competitive in 36. Models using handcrafted features outperform those using raw signal segments in 107 comparisons, highlighting the practical contribution of domain knowledge in noisy, limited-data settings.

Transfer results also depend on the source of training data. Models trained in real-life settings transfer well to laboratory and constrained settings; expert-annotated data support transfer to stimulus-based and self-reported labels. Training with laboratory devices also transfers effectively to tested wearables. Together, these results make dataset differences a central part of evaluating generalization rather than treating performance on one dataset as sufficient evidence.
neurips-2025-feel-quantifying-heterogene.tldr: FEEL compares physiological emotion-recognition methods across 19 datasets to reveal how features, devices, settings, and labels affect generalization.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution and image compression both depend on representing fine visual details effectively. FIPER proposes a shared representation for these tasks called Factorized Features. Its focus is how image information is encoded inside a model, using the same representational idea for increasing resolution and reconstructing compressed images.

The representation decomposes features into bases and coefficients and explicitly describes frequencies. This is intended to capture image structure and visual patterns at multiple scales. The authors replace ordinary feature maps in existing models with Factorized Features to evaluate its broader applicability. For multi-frame compression, they also exploit a mergeable-basis property to consolidate structures shared across frames.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance in the evaluated tasks. The abstract gives an average relative PSNR improvement of 204.4% over the super-resolution baseline and a 9.35% BD-rate reduction relative to the previous compression state of the art. These are distinct task-specific results. Together, they support the paper’s claim that changing the internal representation can benefit both detail reconstruction and compression efficiency.
neurips-2025-fiper-factorized-features-f.tldr: FIPER represents image features through bases, coefficients, and explicit frequencies to improve both super-resolution and compression.

paragraphs: Many optimization algorithms use information from previous updates, with older information receiving progressively less weight. Momentum is one example: it incorporates an exponentially weighted history of gradients. This paper develops a way to understand how such memory changes optimization behavior by approximating an algorithm with a memoryless counterpart.

The construction replaces past iterates in the update rule with the current iterate, then adds a correction that also depends only on the current iterate. That correction captures the effect of memory within the approximation. It can be interpreted as a perturbation of the loss, providing a way to analyze whether memory implicitly regularizes or anti-regularizes the optimization dynamics.

Applying the theory, the authors find that Lion lacks the particular memory-induced anti-regularization they identify in AdamW. They offer this distinction as a theoretical explanation for previously documented better generalization by Lion. Empirical evaluations support the theoretical findings. The result provides an interpretive tool for optimizer behavior while retaining the distinction between an approximate description and the original algorithm.
neurips-2025-how-memory-in-optimization-.tldr: The paper approximates optimizer memory as a change to the loss, helping explain differing generalization behavior in Lion and AdamW.

paragraphs: Humanoid robots with two arms and dexterous hands need demonstrations that coordinate arm motion with detailed hand operations. Existing datasets and simulation benchmarks primarily serve robot-arm platforms, leaving fewer suitable tasks and demonstrations for this more complex setting. HumanoidGen addresses the gap through automated task creation and demonstration collection.

The framework combines atomic dexterous operations with language-model reasoning. It spatially annotates objects and hands around these operations, then uses a language-model planner to produce a sequence of actionable spatial constraints for arm movement. Planning takes account of the scene and the actions objects afford. A variant of Monte Carlo tree search strengthens reasoning for longer tasks and cases with insufficient annotation.

The authors create a benchmark with augmented scenarios to assess the generated data. Their experiments show that the performance of both 2D and 3D diffusion policies can scale with the generated dataset. This supports the framework’s value as a source of training demonstrations, connecting structured task planning to the data needed for coordinated humanoid manipulation.
neurips-2025-humanoidgen-data-generation.tldr: HumanoidGen combines atomic hand operations, spatial constraints, and language-model planning to generate two-handed humanoid manipulation demonstrations.

paragraphs: IPSI addresses structural inference in interacting dynamical systems: learning the relationships underlying the behavior of interacting components. It combines a pretrained structural estimator with a joint inference module based on a variational autoencoder. The two components are updated alternately so that the inferred structure can be progressively refined.

Initially, the structural estimator learns from labels supplied by a meta-dataset or a baseline model. It produces features and structural priors that guide the joint inference module at multiple levels. Later iterations replace those initial labels with pseudolabels generated by the joint module. This creates an iterative exchange between estimating useful structural guidance and using that guidance to improve inference.

The framework is compatible with different VAE-based models. On synthetic physical-system datasets, the authors report significant improvements to structural inference methods, including Neural Relational Inference. Ablations show that feature inputs and structural priors contribute complementary benefits: one strengthens the representation, while the other supports the generative inference process. The findings support combining both forms of guidance within iterative refinement.
neurips-2025-ipsi-enhancing-structural-i.tldr: IPSI alternates structural estimation and VAE-based inference to improve learned interaction structures using progressively refined guidance.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups graph vertices using positive and negative relationships. A disagreement occurs when the grouping conflicts with an edge’s label, and the objective is to minimize these disagreements. This paper studies the streaming setting, where edges arrive in arbitrary order and the algorithm must work within a limited memory budget.

The authors introduce learning-augmented algorithms that use predicted pairwise distances between vertices. Those predictions help improve the tradeoff between storage requirements and clustering quality. The paper treats both complete graphs and general graphs, extending the role of learned guidance to settings with different graph structures.

With sufficiently good predictions, the complete-graph algorithm achieves an approximation factor below three using nearly linear space in the number of vertices. For general graphs, it achieves an O(log |E⁻|) approximation with the same nearly linear space requirement, improving space efficiency over the best-known non-learning method. These guarantees depend on prediction quality. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets also show advantages over the compared non-learning algorithms.
neurips-2025-learning-augmented-streamin.tldr: Predicted vertex distances improve streaming correlation clustering’s memory–accuracy tradeoff when prediction quality is good.

paragraphs: Spatio-temporal forecasts describe how signals change across both locations and time. Real observations can contain noise, anomalies, and shifts that make a trained model’s predictions less reliable. ST-TTC addresses this through learning with calibration during testing, focusing on correcting periodic structural biases that arise as the data change.

Its calibrator operates in the spectral domain and modulates phase and amplitude. This gives it a way to adjust the timing and strength of periodic patterns when predictions become misaligned with current conditions. A flash-updating mechanism uses a streaming memory queue to support efficient updates while predictions are being made.

The approach moves this bias-correction work into the testing phase, bypassing complex training-stage robustness techniques. The authors report real-world experiments supporting its effectiveness, broad applicability, flexibility, and efficiency. The central contribution is a practical mechanism for spending computation on adapting forecasts to changing periodic structure, rather than requiring robustness improvements to come entirely from the original model architecture or training procedure.
neurips-2025-learning-with-calibration-e.tldr: ST-TTC corrects changing periodic biases in spatio-temporal forecasts through efficient spectral calibration at test time.

paragraphs: A generated 3D mesh can have localized defects even when its overall shape appears plausible. Mesh-RFT addresses the difficulty of correcting such defects with rewards assigned only to the whole object. It fine-tunes pretrained mesh generators at the level of individual faces, aiming to improve local quality while preserving the object’s global coherence.

The framework introduces Masked Direct Preference Optimization, which uses quality-aware face masking to enable localized refinement. An accompanying scoring system evaluates geometric integrity and topological regularity at both face and object levels. Its Boundary Edge Ratio and Topology Score provide the quality signals used in the fine-grained training strategy.

Against pretrained models, the reported experiments reduce Hausdorff Distance by 24.6% and improve Topology Score by 3.8%. Against global DPO, they report a 17.4% distance reduction and a 4.9% score gain. These results support the benefit of assigning learning signals to individual mesh faces, with improvements in both geometric fidelity and structural regularity in the evaluated generation setting.
neurips-2025-mesh-rft-enhancing-mesh-gen.tldr: Mesh-RFT uses face-level quality signals and masked preference optimization to improve the geometry and topology of generated meshes.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems often learn from clicks because explicit feedback is expensive to collect. Yet clicking an item does not necessarily mean being satisfied with it: an appealing headline can lead to an unpleasant reading experience. MTRec addresses this mismatch by attempting to infer the satisfaction underlying a user’s observed behavior.

The framework introduces a mental reward model that quantifies inferred user satisfaction. It learns this model through distributional inverse reinforcement learning, then uses the learned rewards to guide sequential recommendation models. The intent is to make recommendations better reflect users’ preferences when implicit interaction signals would otherwise give misleading training guidance.

The authors report significant improvements across several recommendation models. They also deploy MTRec on an industrial short-video platform, where average viewing time increases by 7%. This deployment result demonstrates an improvement in an observed engagement measure. Together with the broader experiments, it supports the usefulness of inferred satisfaction as an additional training signal for recommendation, while the framework’s central target remains alignment with underlying preferences.
neurips-2025-mtrec-learning-to-align-wit.tldr: MTRec learns an inferred satisfaction reward from user behavior to guide recommendations beyond raw click feedback.

paragraphs: A partially observable decision process describes acting when the underlying state cannot be seen directly. This paper adds uncertainty about which process describes the environment. It considers a finite collection of models sharing state, action, and observation spaces, while allowing their transition, observation, and reward rules to differ arbitrarily.

The objective is a single policy that maximizes the worst-case reward across the candidate models. This can represent situations where domain experts disagree about the correct model. The authors show how these multi-environment problems fit into a broader formulation with sets of initial beliefs, called adversarial-belief POMDPs.

They also prove that arbitrary multi-environment problems can be transformed so that uncertainty appears only in transitions and rewards, or only in observations and rewards, while preserving policies and optimal policies. They develop exact and approximate point-based algorithms for the broader formulation. Demonstrations on standard benchmarks extended to multiple environments show that the methods can compute robust policies, connecting the theoretical reformulations to practical policy computation.
neurips-2025-multi-environment-pomdps-di.tldr: The paper develops reformulations and algorithms for policies that maximize worst-case reward across multiple partially observable environment models.

paragraphs: Image stylization must change an image’s appearance while retaining identity, composition, and fine details. Diffusion-based pipelines can lose that consistency, especially in complex scenes, and can weaken the intended style when using style LoRAs. OmniConsistency is a plugin designed to improve content preservation while maintaining the requested visual style.

The method uses large diffusion transformers and learns consistency from aligned image pairs through an in-context framework. Its two-stage progressive training separates style learning from consistency preservation, aiming to reduce style degradation. The resulting plugin is designed to work with arbitrary style LoRAs within the Flux framework, giving the consistency mechanism a reusable role across styles.

The authors report substantial improvements in visual coherence and aesthetic quality, with performance comparable to GPT-4o in their experiments. The contribution is therefore both a training approach and a modular component: paired examples teach what should remain stable, while separating training stages helps keep that stability from interfering with stylization. The compatibility claim is specifically situated within Flux.
neurips-2025-omniconsistency-learning-st.tldr: OmniConsistency learns from aligned image pairs to preserve content and style across Flux stylization pipelines.

paragraphs: This paper studies a classifier that learns from people arriving sequentially, each of whom can pay a cost to alter reported features in pursuit of a favorable decision. The learner announces a binary linear classifier before each interaction. It sees everyone’s reported features but receives true labels only for people assigned the positive class.

Learning therefore combines three obstacles: strategic changes to inputs, selectively observed labels, and noisy outcomes. The analysis assumes the underlying feature-label distribution follows a halfspace model with Massart noise. This allows bounded label noise to depend arbitrarily on the features, making the stated noise assumption part of the scope of the result.

The authors propose an algorithm whose classifiers converge to the clairvoyant optimum under this setup. They also establish regret growing as O(√T), apart from polylogarithmic and constant factors, over T interactions. This gives a quantitative guarantee that accumulated performance loss grows sublinearly, despite manipulation and incomplete feedback. The result concerns learning under the combined modeled challenges rather than treating each in isolation.
neurips-2025-online-strategic-classifica.tldr: An online classifier achieves convergence and sublinear regret despite strategic feature manipulation, positive-only label feedback, and bounded feature-dependent noise.

paragraphs: Physical knowledge can help reconstruct complex environmental signals, but available laws may describe only part of what drives the observations. Ocean surface chlorophyll concentration illustrates this problem: both physical and biological processes influence it, while the biological contribution is poorly constrained. Treating the known physics as a complete description can therefore misrepresent the system.

The proposed Partial Physics Informed Diffusion Model incorporates known principles through a physics operator. It also minimizes discrepancies associated with unknown dynamics to reduce their impact. This design explicitly accommodates incomplete physical knowledge, allowing the model to use the constraints that are available without assuming they account for all observed behavior.

The authors demonstrate the framework on ocean surface chlorophyll data. Experiments report substantially improved prediction accuracy and stability relative to methods that ignore physics and methods that impose incomplete constraints as though they were complete. The findings support incorporating partial physical knowledge in a way that acknowledges unresolved dynamics, making the treatment of uncertainty in the physical description central to the approach.
neurips-2025-partial-physics-informed-di.tldr: PPIDM improves ocean chlorophyll reconstruction by incorporating known physics while accounting for incompletely understood dynamics.

paragraphs: This study examines how a text’s position affects the extraction of memorized training content. The authors train 1B-, 3B-, and 8B-parameter language models from scratch on 83B tokens, mixing web data with public-domain books used to simulate copyrighted material at controlled frequencies. This provides a controlled setting for investigating verbatim recall.

They identify an offset effect: short prefixes from the beginning of the context window trigger the strongest memorization, while longer prefixes can reduce it. Recall also drops sharply when the prefix starts away from the initial tokens. The authors attribute this sensitivity to positional fragility, in which early tokens serve disproportionately as retrieval anchors.

Failed retrieval often accompanies degenerated text. In the reported experiments, shifting sensitive material deeper into the context suppresses both extractable memorization and degeneration. These findings identify positional offset as an important evaluation variable: probing only document or sequence beginnings can miss how strongly recall depends on placement. The evidence concerns suppression of extractable recall, rather than establishing that the underlying memorized content has been removed.
neurips-2025-positional-fragility-in-llm.tldr: Controlled training experiments show that verbatim recall can depend sharply on prefix position, making positional offset important for memorization evaluation.

paragraphs: Spending more computation during answering can improve language-model reasoning, but deterministic search may discard promising partial solutions too early. The paper identifies imperfect reward models as a cause: a useful trajectory can receive a poor intermediate assessment and disappear before its potential becomes clear.

Rollout Roulette adapts particle-based Monte Carlo methods to inference-time reasoning. It maintains a diverse collection of candidate trajectories and balances exploration with exploitation. This probabilistic approach addresses the risk of committing too strongly to early judgments, connecting language-model search with methods developed for probabilistic inference.

The authors report a 4–16-fold better scaling rate than deterministic search counterparts across evaluated mathematical and broader reasoning tasks. They also report that Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct surpasses GPT-4o accuracy with four rollouts, while the 7B model reaches o1-level accuracy with 32 rollouts in their evaluation. These comparisons describe the tested reasoning settings. The central finding is that preserving and probabilistically managing alternatives can make additional inference computation more productive.
neurips-2025-rollout-roulette-a-probabil.tldr: Rollout Roulette uses particle-based probabilistic search to retain diverse reasoning paths and improve the returns from inference-time computation.

paragraphs: Retrieval can extend a language model’s available knowledge, but retrieved material may be irrelevant or noisy. AutoRefine addresses how a model processes evidence while reasoning, introducing explicit refinement steps between successive searches. The goal is to make external information more useful before the model commits to an answer.

The framework trains the model to filter, distill, and organize evidence throughout the search process. It uses reinforcement learning after initial model training, combining rewards tailored to retrieval with rewards for answer correctness. Group relative policy optimization supports this training, linking the quality of information gathering to the final result.

Experiments on questions requiring either one retrieval step or multiple linked steps show significant improvements over existing approaches, especially for complex multi-hop reasoning. Further analysis finds frequent, higher-quality searches and effective evidence synthesis. The results support making evidence refinement an explicit learned operation within reasoning: the model is encouraged to improve what it knows between searches, helping it combine information into a more accurate answer.
neurips-2025-search-and-refine-during-th.tldr: AutoRefine trains language models to refine retrieved evidence between searches, improving retrieval-augmented reasoning, especially on multi-hop questions.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a pretrained LiDAR world model can transfer beyond its original domain. It studies outdoor-to-indoor transfer, adaptation from sparse to dense sensor beams, and transfer from non-semantic learning to semantic prediction. The experiments vary the amount of fine-tuning data to assess the usefulness of shared pretraining.

A single pretrained model beats training from scratch in 30 of 36 comparisons, with gains reaching 11% absolute improvement, or 83% relative improvement. For semantic occupancy forecasting, the method exceeds previous baselines using only 5% of their labeled training data. These findings show substantial transfer benefits across the evaluated scenarios, though the comparison count also makes clear that gains are not universal.

The authors additionally introduce a latent conditional flow-matching framework to address inefficient compression and training objectives. It achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction with half the training data and six times the compression ratio of prior methods. Semantic occupancy forecasting also reaches state-of-the-art performance, with reported computational-efficiency gains of 1.98–23 times and throughput gains of 1.1–3.9 times.
neurips-2025-towards-foundational-lidar-.tldr: A transfer study and latent flow-matching framework show how LiDAR world models can reuse pretraining while improving data and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: White-matter tractography reconstructs three-dimensional brain pathways from diffusion MRI measurements. The task resembles pathfinding through noisy, ambiguous evidence, especially where fibers cross, merge, or fan out. TractoTransformer addresses this ambiguity by combining information about a streamline’s trajectory with measurements around its current location.

A Transformer models the sequence of the streamline, using trajectory context together with current diffusion measurements to predict fiber directions. A convolutional neural network extracts local microstructural features from neighborhoods around each voxel. These components provide complementary information: the path’s sequential context and the surrounding spatial evidence both contribute to the next direction prediction.

The authors report improved precision and completeness relative to traditional tractography models. Evaluation with the Tractometer toolkit yields competitive performance against state-of-the-art approaches, while qualitative results on TractoInferno demonstrate strong generalization to real-world data. The contribution is a combined sequential and spatial model for tracing pathways, with the quantitative claim framed as competitive performance and the real-data evidence presented qualitatively.
neurips-2025-tractotransformer-diffusion.tldr: TractoTransformer combines streamline history and local MRI features to improve white-matter pathway reconstruction.
